recent_posts.title: Parsing with an MCAP Index — Monday Morning Haskell
recent_posts.summary: This tutorial demonstrates how to parse MCAP bag files using indexing to achieve 75x faster performance compared to sequential parsing. It walks through parsing footer records, summary offsets, chunk indexes, and message indexes to efficiently extract specific topic messages from ROS2 bag files. The implementation uses Haskell's Megaparsec library with custom monad stacks (StateT, ReaderT, ExceptT) to manage file seeking and state. The approach works with uncompressed chunks and shows how to navigate the MCAP format's index structure to jump directly to desired messages rather than reading the entire file sequentially.

recent_posts.title: Serializing an HTTP Response & Running the Server — Monday Morning Haskell
recent_posts.summary: This tutorial concludes a three-part series on building an HTTP server from scratch in Haskell. It covers creating HTTP responses with appropriate status codes and headers, serializing response objects into ByteStrings using helper functions, and implementing the networking layer using Network.Socket and Network.Run.TCP. The guide demonstrates handling client connections, parsing requests with Megaparsec, generating responses, and sending data back through sockets. Complete working code is provided for a basic server that returns 200 OK or 400 Bad Request responses.

recent_posts.title: Parsing an HTTP Request — Monday Morning Haskell
recent_posts.summary: A step-by-step guide to building an HTTP request parser in Haskell using the Megaparsec library. Demonstrates parsing HTTP methods, URIs, versions, headers, and request bodies by combining top-down design with bottom-up implementation. Covers helper functions for handling ByteString conversions, character parsing, and CRLF sequences, culminating in a complete parser that follows the HTTP/1.1 RFC specification.

recent_posts.title: Stock Market Shark: More Multidimensional DP — Monday Morning Haskell
recent_posts.summary: Explores solving the LeetCode 'Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV' problem using multidimensional dynamic programming in both Rust and Haskell. The problem involves maximizing profit from stock transactions with constraints on simultaneous holdings. The solution uses a 2D grid where dimensions represent transaction states and days, with Rust implementing a full grid approach while Haskell optimizes memory by maintaining only necessary rows. Demonstrates how functional programming patterns in Haskell can achieve the same algorithmic results with different implementation strategies compared to imperative approaches.

recent_posts.title: Spatial DP: Finding the Largest Square — Monday Morning Haskell
recent_posts.summary: Explores solving the Maximal Square problem using dynamic programming across two dimensions. The solution builds layers representing squares of increasing size, checking if each cell can be the top-left corner of a k×k square by validating four adjacent cells from the previous layer. Implementations are provided in both Rust (using mutable arrays) and Haskell (using immutable HashMaps), demonstrating different approaches to spatial DP optimization.

recent_posts.title: Making Change: Array-Based DP — Monday Morning Haskell
recent_posts.summary: Explores the classic coin change problem using dynamic programming with array-based solutions. Demonstrates how to build a DP array where each index represents the minimum coins needed for that amount, starting from a base case of zero. Provides complete implementations in both Rust (using mutable vectors) and Haskell (using immutable IntMap), highlighting the differences in handling array mutations between imperative and functional approaches. Explains why greedy algorithms fail for this problem and walks through the logic of looking back in the array based on coin values to find optimal solutions.

recent_posts.title: Dynamic Programming Primer — Monday Morning Haskell
recent_posts.summary: Explores dynamic programming through the House Robber problem, comparing implementations in Haskell and Rust. Explains the tabulation approach where you build solutions from base cases upward, tracking maximum values for robbed and unrobbed states. The Haskell solution uses recursion with constant memory, while Rust uses an iterative loop. Both achieve O(1) space complexity by only storing the previous two states instead of full arrays.

recent_posts.title: Apply the Trie: Word Search — Monday Morning Haskell
recent_posts.summary: Demonstrates solving LeetCode's Word Search II problem by combining Trie data structures with Depth First Search algorithms. The solution efficiently finds multiple words in a character grid using Boggle-style movement rules. Includes complete implementations in both Haskell and Rust, showing how to optimize prefix searching with Tries and implement backtracking for grid traversal.

recent_posts.title: In-Order Traversal in Haskell and Rust — Monday Morning Haskell
recent_posts.summary: Demonstrates implementing in-order traversal for finding the k-th smallest element in a binary search tree using both Haskell and Rust. The algorithm uses a stack-based approach to traverse nodes from smallest to largest value, handling the complexities of Rust's RefCell and Rc wrappers for memory management while showing cleaner recursive patterns in Haskell.

recent_posts.title: Implementing binary tree inversion in Rust, Haskell, and C++
recent_posts.summary: Explores implementing a binary tree inversion algorithm across different programming languages, highlighting how Rust's ownership model and memory safety features make recursive data structures more complex compared to Haskell and C++. The article demonstrates the same algorithm in three languages, showing how Rust requires wrapper types like RefCell, Rc, and Option to handle memory management safely, while Haskell uses simple pattern matching and C++ relies on raw pointers.
